\chapter{The Marks Themselves}
\label{ch:signos}
\hlchaptermodality{424}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name eight Spanish punctuation marks, say what each one does to a sentence, and write a short note that uses six of them correctly.}

Write a short note that opens with a colon after the name, lists three things without a comma before the final y, carries an aside in parentheses and an address abbreviated with a slash.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el punto]{el punto — the mark you have read ten thousand times and never been told about}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-punto}



\begin{quote}
Look at the last sentence you read. It ended in a mark. Say what that mark is called in Spanish before reading on — and notice that this book has printed it on every page without once naming it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el punto} — \textquotedblleft{}the full stop,\textquotedblright{} or in American English, the period.

Spanish gives the same mark a different name according to what follows it, and those names appear in exam instructions, so they are worth having:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what comes next} & \textbf{name} & \textbf{what it closes} \\
\midrule
another sentence, same paragraph & \textbf{punto y seguido} & a sentence \\
a new paragraph & \textbf{punto y aparte} & a paragraph \\
nothing & \textbf{punto final} & the whole text \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The mark on the page is identical in all three. What changes is the size of the thing being finished — a sentence, a block, or a text. \emph{Seguido} means \textquotedblleft{}continued,\textquotedblright{} \emph{aparte} means \textquotedblleft{}separate,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{final} means what it looks like.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: spacing, and the one place the mark is left off}]
Two mechanical habits that a written paper is marked on:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{correct} & \textbf{wrong} \\
\midrule
spacing & \texttt{Hola. Adiós.} & \texttt{Hola .Adiós.} \\
after a title & \texttt{Mi familia} & \texttt{Mi familia.} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No space before the point, one space after it. And a \textbf{title or a heading takes no point at all} — which is why every heading in this book ends bare.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el punto\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of the three names a point gets when a new paragraph follows (\emph{punto y aparte})
  \item whether the title of your exam answer should end in a point (no)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference on the page between \emph{punto y seguido} and \emph{punto y aparte}? (Nothing — the mark is the same; what follows it differs.) Where does the space go? (After the point, not before.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la coma]{la coma — where Spanish and English disagree about lists}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-coma}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el punto}. This mark is its smaller relative: it divides without finishing.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la coma} — \textquotedblleft{}the comma.\textquotedblright{} From Greek \emph{kómma}, \textquotedblleft{}a piece cut off,\textquotedblright{} which is what a comma does to a sentence.

In a list, the items are divided by commas — and \textbf{in front of the final \emph{y}, Spanish writes no comma}:

\begin{quote}
Tengo un hermano, una hermana \textbf{y} un perro.
\end{quote}

English allows \emph{a brother, a sister, and a dog}. Spanish does not put a comma there. This is one of the few orthographic points where a habit carried from English is visible to a marker.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: when y becomes e, and o becomes u}]
The joining word itself changes shape to avoid two identical vowel sounds colliding:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{becomes} & \textbf{before a word starting with} \\
\midrule
y & \textbf{e} & \emph{i-} or \emph{hi-} \\
o & \textbf{u} & \emph{o-} or \emph{ho-} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item padres \textbf{e} hijos — parents and children
  \item siete \textbf{u} ocho — seven or eight
\end{itemize}

You met this already without being told its name: \emph{simpática \textbf{e} inteligente} in the character chapter changed for exactly this reason.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la coma\textquotedblright{}
  \item a list of three things, and stop yourself before putting a comma in front of the \emph{y}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}padres e hijos\textquotedblright{}, and why it is not \emph{y hijos}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}siete u ocho\textquotedblright{}, and why it is not \emph{o ocho}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Spanish put a comma before the final \emph{y} of a list? (No.) What does \emph{y} become before \emph{hijos}? (\emph{E}.) What does \emph{o} become before \emph{ocho}? (\emph{U}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[los dos puntos]{los dos puntos — a plural name, and the mark that opens a letter}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-dos-puntos}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la coma}. The next mark also introduces a list — but it stands in front of the list rather than inside it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{los dos puntos} — \textquotedblleft{}the colon.\textquotedblright{} Spanish names it for what it looks like: \textbf{two points}, and the name is plural, so it takes \emph{los} and a plural verb.

Its main job is to \textbf{announce} what follows:

\begin{quote}
Tengo tres colores favoritos: rojo, azul y verde.
\end{quote}

The colon promises a list; the commas then divide it; and there is still no comma before the final \emph{y}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the letter opening, where English disagrees}]
This is the exam-relevant half, because a written paper often asks for a note or a message:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{opening} \\
\midrule
Spanish & Querido Juan\textbf{:} \\
English & Dear John\textbf{,} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish puts \textbf{dos puntos} after the greeting of a letter, an email or a note. English puts a comma. A Spanish reader notices the comma immediately, the way an English reader notices a colon.

After it, the text begins on the next line, and it begins with a \textbf{capital}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}los dos puntos\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{los}, because the name is plural
  \item a sentence that announces a list of three things and then gives it
  \item how you would open a note to a friend called Ana (\emph{Querida Ana:})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is the name plural? (There are two points in the mark.) What goes after \emph{Querido Juan} in Spanish? (A colon, where English uses a comma.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la raya]{la raya — you have been reading this mark for chapters}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-raya}



\begin{quote}
Every printed conversation you have read in this book opened its lines with a long horizontal mark. Name what it was doing there, before reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la raya} — \textquotedblleft{}the dash.\textquotedblright{} A \emph{raya} is a line or a stripe, and it is longer than the hyphen, which is a different mark with a different job.

In printed Spanish dialogue, a \textbf{raya opens each turn of speech}, and nobody is named:

\begin{quote}
— ¿Cómo estás? — Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? — Muy bien.
\end{quote}

Three turns, two speakers, no \emph{he said} and no quotation marks. The reader tracks who is talking by alternation alone.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what replaces the quotation marks}]
Set the two traditions side by side, because a reading paper prints the Spanish one and an English-trained eye looks for the wrong thing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
opens a turn & \textquotedblleft{}Hello,\textquotedblright{} & — Hola. \\
names the speaker & he said & often nobody \\
new speaker & new paragraph & new paragraph \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An English reader hunting for quotation marks in a Spanish story finds none and concludes there is no dialogue. There is; it is marked with \textbf{la raya}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la raya\textquotedblright{}
  \item how a reader knows who is speaking when nobody is named (the turns alternate)
  \item what an English reader is looking for that will not be there (quotation marks)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What opens a turn of speech in printed Spanish? (\emph{La raya}.) How many speakers are named in a typical exchange? (Often none.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[las comillas]{las comillas — three shapes, and the preferred one points outward}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-comillas}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson said a Spanish dialogue carries no quotation marks. So Spanish does have them — they are for something else. This lesson says what.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{las comillas} — \textquotedblleft{}quotation marks.\textquotedblright{} Plural, like \emph{los dos puntos}, because they come as a pair.

Spanish uses three shapes and puts them in an order of preference:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{name} & \textbf{when} \\
\midrule
« » & comillas latinas, or angulares & preferred in printed Spanish \\
" " & comillas inglesas & inside a quotation already in « » \\
' ' & comillas simples & inside that again \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The outermost pair is the angular one. Nesting works from the outside in, so the English-looking pair appears \textbf{inside} the Spanish-looking one, rather than first.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what they are actually for}]
Since \textbf{la raya} already handles dialogue, the marks are free for other work, and the one an A1 paper shows is the \textbf{foreign word}:

\begin{quote}
El camarero trajo un «sandwich».
\end{quote}

A word borrowed and not yet naturalised is set apart from the sentence around it. Spanish also uses them for a title inside a text, and for a word being talked about rather than used.

The name is a diminutive of \textbf{coma}: a \emph{comilla} is a small comma, which is what the mark once looked like.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}las comillas\textquotedblright{}, plural, with \emph{las}
  \item which shape a printed Spanish text reaches for first (« »)
  \item what the name is a small version of (\emph{coma})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which pair does printed Spanish prefer? (The angular « ».) Why are they not needed for dialogue? (\emph{La raya} marks the turns instead.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[los paréntesis]{los paréntesis — a putting-in-beside}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-parentesis}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{las comillas}. The next mark also sets something apart from the sentence — but what it sets apart is an aside rather than a quotation.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{los paréntesis} — \textquotedblleft{}the parentheses,\textquotedblright{} the curved pair.

The word is Greek and it describes the job precisely: \textbf{para-} beside, \textbf{en-} in, \textbf{thesis} a putting. A \emph{parénthesis} is \emph{a putting-in-beside} — a remark placed next to the sentence rather than inside its grammar.

\begin{quote}
Mi hermana (la mayor) vive en Madrid.
\end{quote}

Remove what is between them and the sentence still stands: \emph{Mi hermana vive en Madrid.} That is the test for whether the mark is the right one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: spacing, and where the point goes}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{correct} & \textbf{wrong} \\
\midrule
spacing & \texttt{casa (grande) blanca} & \texttt{casa ( grande ) blanca} \\
with a point & \texttt{... en Madrid.} & \texttt{... en Madrid).} inside \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No space on the inside of either curve. And when a parenthesis closes at the end of a sentence, the point goes \textbf{outside} it — the aside finishes first, then the sentence does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}los paréntesis\textquotedblright{}
  \item what the three Greek pieces mean (beside, in, a putting)
  \item the test for whether an aside belongs in them (remove it, and see whether the sentence still stands)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Greek word literally describe? (A putting-in-beside.) Where does the full stop go at the end of a sentence that closes with a parenthesis? (Outside it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el guion]{el guion — the short one, and why it is not la raya}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-guion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la raya}. This lesson gives you a mark that looks like a small version of it and does something completely different.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el guion} — \textquotedblleft{}the hyphen.\textquotedblright{}

The two marks are easy to confuse on a page and easy to keep apart once you know what each is for:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{length} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
la raya & long & opens a turn of speech \\
el guion & short & \textbf{joins} two words into one \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Its everyday A1 use is in names:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Ana-María} — a compound forename
  \item \textbf{Sánchez-Pérez} — a compound surname, often a married name or a double family name
\end{itemize}

A form asking for \emph{apellidos} may come back with a hyphen in it, and the hyphen is telling you the two halves are one name rather than two.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word changed its own spelling}]
This one is a small piece of history you will see both ways in print:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{spelling} & \textbf{status} \\
\midrule
guión & the older form, with a written accent \\
\textbf{guion} & the current recommendation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The Academy reclassified \emph{guion} as a one-syllable word in 2010, and a one-syllable word carries no written accent. Older books print \emph{guión} and are not wrong for their date. Both will appear in front of you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el guion\textquotedblright{}
  \item the difference between what \emph{la raya} does and what \emph{el guion} does
  \item a compound surname with a hyphen in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two marks opens a line of dialogue? (\emph{La raya}, the long one.) Why does the current spelling \emph{guion} carry no accent? (It is counted as one syllable.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la barra]{la barra — a choice, a street, and a speed limit}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-barra}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el guion}, the mark that joins. This one separates — and what it separates are usually alternatives.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la barra} — \textquotedblleft{}the slash.\textquotedblright{} A \emph{barra} is a bar or a rod, named for its shape.

Three jobs, all of which turn up on an A1 reading paper:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{use} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{reading} \\
\midrule
alternatives & y/o & and, or both \\
abbreviation & c/ Mayor & \emph{calle} Mayor \\
per & km/h & kilometres per hour \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The middle one is the useful surprise: \textbf{c/} on a Spanish address is \emph{calle}, the street. An envelope, a form or a shop sign will print it that way, and it is unreadable if nobody has told you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the mark that means \textquotedblleft{}per\textquotedblright{}}]
In a measurement, \emph{la barra} is read aloud as \textbf{por}:

\begin{quote}
50 km/h — \emph{cincuenta kilómetros por hora}
\end{quote}

It is not silent and it is not spelled out. A listening paper that reads a speed limit aloud gives you \emph{por} where the page shows a slash.

No spaces around it in any of these uses.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la barra\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \textbf{c/} stands for on an address (\emph{calle})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}50 km/h\textquotedblright{} the way it is read aloud
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{c/} abbreviate? (\emph{Calle}.) What word replaces the slash when a measurement is read aloud? (\emph{Por}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ocho signos]{ocho signos — sorted by what each one does to a sentence}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-repaso-signos}



\begin{quote}
Name as many of the eight marks as you can, in Spanish, before reading the table. Aim for five.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: divide, join, or set apart}]
Eight marks, and every one of them is doing one of three jobs:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{name} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
. & el punto & divides — a sentence, a paragraph, a text \\
, & la coma & divides — inside a sentence \\
: & los dos puntos & divides — and announces what follows \\
— & la raya & sets apart — a turn of speech \\
« » & las comillas & sets apart — a quoted or foreign word \\
( ) & los paréntesis & sets apart — an aside \\
- & el guion & \textbf{joins} — two words into one name \\
/ & la barra & divides — alternatives, or \emph{per} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Seven divide or set apart. \textbf{El guion} is the only one of the eight that joins, which is the cleanest way to keep it from being confused with the mark it most resembles.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three with plural names}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{name} & \textbf{why plural} \\
\midrule
los dos puntos & two points in the mark \\
las comillas & they come as a pair \\
los paréntesis & so do these \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Each of the three is one mark to an English speaker and a plural noun in Spanish, so each takes \emph{los} or \emph{las} and a plural verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three with plural names, with their articles
  \item the one that joins rather than divides (\emph{el guion})
  \item the one that opens a line of dialogue (\emph{la raya})
  \item the one Spanish leaves out in front of the final \emph{y} of a list (\emph{la coma})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the eight joins? (\emph{El guion}.) Which two are both horizontal lines with different lengths and different jobs? (\emph{La raya} and \emph{el guion}.) Which one is read aloud as \emph{por}? (\emph{La barra}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[una nota con todos los signos]{una nota con todos los signos — the marks doing their jobs at once}

\label{lesson:ES-C424-sintesis-nota}



\begin{quote}
Say how a Spanish note opens after the name, and say whether a list of three takes a comma before its \emph{y}.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read this note and count the marks. Every word in it has been taught:

\begin{quote}
Querida Ana:
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Mañana voy al teatro con mi hermana (la mayor). Vamos a ver una película, una exposición y un concierto. Mi dirección es c/ Mayor, 5.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Un abrazo, Marta
\end{quote}

Six of the eight marks are at work: the colon after the name, commas inside the list with none before the \emph{y}, a parenthesis around the aside, a slash in the address, and points closing the sentences.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
And the two the note had no use for, doing their own jobs:

\begin{quote}
— ¿Vamos al cine? — Sí. Traigo un «sandwich».
\end{quote}

The first line opens with \textbf{la raya} because it is a turn of speech. The borrowed word sits inside \textbf{las comillas} because it is not naturalised.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the mark that opens the note after \emph{Querida Ana}
  \item the list of three from the note, and stop before the \emph{y} without putting a comma there
  \item what \textbf{c/} is short for
  \item which mark would open the note if it were a line of dialogue instead
  \item what a hyphen in \emph{Sánchez-Pérez} is telling you (that the two halves are one name)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the point go when a sentence ends with a parenthesis? (Outside it.) Which mark marks the foreign word, and which marks the turn of speech? (\emph{Las comillas} and \emph{la raya}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
